# Before running the code

Open `poli210-seminar8.Rproj` in RStudio, then open this document. Keep the
`data` and `R` folders beside it. Paths such as `data/ug.csv` are relative to
this project folder, on both macOS and Windows. Do not use a path to the
instructor's computer or move the QMD away from its data.

Install these packages **once**, in the Console if needed:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "readr", "stringr"))
```

Load packages and data **each new R session**. Run this setup before jumping
to an example. The later join and reshape examples build on their preceding
chunks. Rendering runs everything in order in a fresh session.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)

elections <- read_csv("data/elections.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ug <- read_csv("data/ug.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
turk <- read_csv("data/mturk.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
states <- read_csv("data/states.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
members <- read_csv("data/house114.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
options(width = 85, pillar.width = 85)
```

`read_csv()` is from **readr** and returns a tibble. `filter()` and the other
data verbs are from **dplyr**; pivoting is from **tidyr**; text tools are from
**stringr**. These packages belong to the tidyverse. `library(tidyverse)`
is an alternative that loads these and several more packages.

No download is needed during class. The local CSVs are frozen teaching copies.
`source("R/setup.R")` reloads the original input objects if you want to start over.

# 1. What does one row represent?

## The ultimatum game

`ug` contains 234 participants: 102 elites and 132 undergraduates. Each person
provided a proposal and a minimum acceptable offer (MAO), when recorded.
These are different choices by the same respondent, not an observed matched pair.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `participant_id` | Teaching ID tied to a row in the source file |
| `population`, `elite` | Sample label; `elite` is 1 for elites and 0 for undergraduates |
| `mao`, `offer` | Minimum acceptable offer and proposed offer, on a 0–100 scale |
| `age` | Age in years |
| `levelk`, `patience` | Original reasoning and patience measures |
| `experience` | Experience in years, collected for elites only |

Unlike B2's prepared file, this table **keeps missing MAOs** and additional
variables. A zero MAO is a valid response, not missing. The original incentives
involved lotteries; we continue to use the simplified 100-point interpretation.

```{r}
ug
glimpse(ug)
dim(ug)
names(ug)
```

A tibble's truncated display is not a subset of the data. `head()` displays a
small subset; `as_tibble()` converts an ordinary data frame to a tibble.

```{r}
as_tibble(as.data.frame(ug)) %>% head(n = 3)
```

## The elections

`elections` has one row per retained district-election, 9,337 rows across
28 election years from 1946 through 2014. It is the selected CSV used in the
old course, **not all House elections**. For example, it has 328 races in 2014,
not 435. Some election years are absent. Do not interpret its mean as a
national popular-vote share or its counts as national seat totals.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `year`, `stcd` | Election year and original state-district code |
| `state` | State number in alphabetical order, **not FIPS or ICPSR** |
| `dv`, `dvp` | Democratic two-party House vote percentage, current/prior election |
| `dpres` | Democratic two-party presidential vote percentage; for midterms, two years earlier |
| `inc3` | 1 Democratic incumbent, −1 Republican incumbent, 0 no incumbent |
| `ptynow` | Party holding the seat before the election: 1 D, −1 R, 0 neither/new |
| `south` | 1 for an old-Confederacy state, 0 otherwise |
| `source_row` | Row in the local source CSV, not a substantive variable |

The original archive treats unopposed races as missing for `dv`. All `dv`
and `dvp` values in this selected CSV are observed. Missing `dpres` values remain.

```{r}
elections %>% select(year, stcd, inc3, dv, dvp) %>% head()
elections %>% count(year) %>% print(n = 30)
```

# 2. Verbs and pipes

## Keep rows with `filter()`

```{r}
filter(elections, year == 2014, inc3 == 0)
```

Commas between conditions mean **AND**. Use `|` for OR and `%in%` for membership.
Use `==` to compare values, not `=`. Column names are unquoted inside these
verbs; literal text values are quoted.

```{r}
ug %>% filter(population == "Elites", mao >= 50) %>% head()
elections %>% filter(year %in% c(2010, 2014)) %>% head()
ug %>% filter(mao < 20 | mao > 50) %>% head()
```

`filter()` keeps conditions that evaluate to `TRUE`. It drops both `FALSE`
and `NA`. Test missingness with `is.na()`, never `mao == NA`.

```{r}
ug %>% filter(is.na(mao)) %>% select(participant_id, population, mao)
```

## Select and rename columns

```{r}
select(ug, participant_id, population, mao, offer) %>% head()
ug %>% select(-experience) %>% head(n = 2)

elections %>%
  select(year, stcd, dv, dvp) %>%
  rename(dem_vote = dv, prior_dem_vote = dvp) %>%
  head()
```

`rename(new_name = old_name)` retains other columns. `select()` chooses which
columns remain. Printing either result does **not** overwrite the input.

## Read a pipe as “then”

```{r}
open_2014 <- elections %>%
  filter(year == 2014, inc3 == 0) %>%
  select(year, stcd, dv, dvp) %>%
  arrange(desc(dv))
open_2014
```

`x %>% f(y)` usually means `f(x, y)`. The book uses `%>%`; the native R pipe
`|>` works for these examples too. The assignment arrow saves the result.

## Sort versus choose the largest/smallest

```{r}
elections %>% filter(year == 2014) %>% arrange(dv) %>% head()
elections %>% filter(year == 2014) %>% slice_max(dv, n = 3)
elections %>% filter(year == 2014) %>% slice_min(dv, n = 3)
```

`arrange()` reorders all rows. `slice_max()`/`slice_min()` retain selected
rows; ties are included by default, so `n = 3` can return more than three.
`with_ties = FALSE` caps the result, but it does not provide a substantive
reason to prefer one tied case. These are the largest/smallest Democratic
vote percentages **in this selected sample**.

## Compute columns with `mutate()`

```{r}
elections_derived <- elections %>%
  mutate(
    dem_share = dv / 100,
    dem_swing = dv - dvp,
    distance_from_50 = abs(dv - 50),
    incumbent = inc3 != 0
  )
elections_derived %>%
  select(year, stcd, dv, dem_share, dem_swing, incumbent) %>% head()
```

`dem_share` is a proportion. `dem_swing` is a **percentage-point** change.
Do not call `abs(dv - 50)` the two-candidate victory margin: that margin is
`abs(2 * dv - 100)` percentage points. Neither is a causal incumbency effect.

## Conditional transformations

`mutate()` can create logical flags and readable categories, as well as
arithmetic transformations. `if_else(condition, yes, no)` chooses a value
for each row. `case_when()` checks alternatives in order; the first match wins.

```{r}
ug_flags <- ug %>% mutate(
  mao_missing = is.na(mao),
  offers_half_or_more = offer >= 50,
  sample_label = if_else(elite == 1, "Elite", "Undergraduate")
)
elections_labels <- elections %>% mutate(
  incumbent_party = case_when(
    inc3 == 1 ~ "Democratic incumbent",
    inc3 == -1 ~ "Republican incumbent",
    inc3 == 0 ~ "No incumbent",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
)
ug_flags %>% select(participant_id, mao, mao_missing, offers_half_or_more) %>% head()
```

These labels follow the source codebook, not an assumption that every numeric
code has a self-evident meaning. `sample_label` is specific to the two-sample
`ug` table: it would mislabel MTurk respondents if used after appending them.

## Missing responses and worst-case bounds

How much could the unobserved MAOs change the mean among **all 102 elites**?
First check the data, rather than assuming which variable is missing:

```{r}
ug %>% group_by(population) %>% summarize(
  n_total = n(),
  missing_mao = sum(is.na(mao)),
  missing_offer = sum(is.na(offer)), .groups = "drop"
)
```

Four elite MAOs are missing; elite offers are all observed. Two undergraduate
MAOs are missing. For each variable, preserve observed values and replace only
missing values by the endpoints of its allowed 0–100 range.

```{r}
ug_bounds <- ug %>% mutate(
  mao_lower = if_else(is.na(mao), 0, mao),
  mao_upper = if_else(is.na(mao), 100, mao),
  offer_lower = if_else(is.na(offer), 0, offer),
  offer_upper = if_else(is.na(offer), 100, offer)
)
ug_bounds %>%
  filter(elite == 1, is.na(mao)) %>%
  select(participant_id, mao, mao_lower, mao_upper, offer, offer_lower, offer_upper)
```

`coalesce(x, replacement)` is a compact alternative: take `x` when observed,
otherwise take the replacement. Thus `coalesce(mao, 0)` produces the same
lower-bound variable. It is different from replacing every value by zero.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(ug_bounds$mao_lower, coalesce(ug$mao, 0)))
elite_bounds <- ug_bounds %>% filter(elite == 1) %>% summarize(
  n_total = n(),
  n_observed = sum(!is.na(mao)),
  observed_mao_mean = mean(mao, na.rm = TRUE),
  full_sample_lower = mean(mao_lower),
  full_sample_upper = mean(mao_upper),
  offer_lower_mean = mean(offer_lower),
  offer_upper_mean = mean(offer_upper)
)
elite_bounds
```

The observed-case MAO mean uses 98 people. Both bounds use all 102. If `m`
responses are missing out of `N`, the full-sample mean lies in

$$
\left[\frac{\sum_{i:\,M_i\text{ observed}} M_i}{N},
\quad \frac{\sum_{i:\,M_i\text{ observed}} M_i+100m}{N}\right].
$$

For elites the bounds are about **29.4 to 33.4**, a width of
`100 * 4 / 102`, or 3.92 points. The observed-case mean is about 30.6.
Both offer bounds equal the observed offer mean, about 43.0, because there
are no missing offers in this table.

These are **worst-case bounds for this finite sample**, assuming the missing
values are in [0, 100] and observed values are correct. They are not confidence
intervals, population bounds, or claims that anyone actually chose 0 or 100.
We do not need to assume the responses are missing at random for these bounds.
The original `mao` and `offer` columns remain unchanged.

We will return to `summarize()` and `group_by()` just below. **Try it then:**
compute the same MAO bounds separately for elites and undergraduates. Which
group has wider bounds, and how does that follow from its missing fraction?

## Unique values with `distinct()`

```{r}
ug %>% distinct(population)
elections %>% distinct(year, stcd) %>% nrow()
ug %>% distinct(mao) %>% nrow()
```

The last command counts distinct MAO values, including `NA`, **not people**.
Never deduplicate participants just because they chose the same MAO.

**Try it:** Among the retained 2014 races, find the five closest to 50%.
Show year, district code, Democratic vote percentage, and distance from 50%.
Start from `elections_derived`; combine `filter()`, `slice_min()`, and `select()`.

# 3. Summaries, groups, and missing values

## Collapse to a summary row

```{r}
ug %>% summarize(mean_mao = mean(mao))
ug %>% summarize(
  n_rows = n(),
  n_mao = sum(!is.na(mao)),
  n_missing = sum(is.na(mao)),
  mean_mao = mean(mao, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd_mao = sd(mao, na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

`summarise()` and `summarize()` are the same function. `n()` counts rows,
including rows with missing MAO. `na.rm = TRUE` uses observed values for that
calculation; it does not delete rows or make nonresponse harmless.

## Repeat the same calculation within groups

```{r}
ug_summary <- ug %>%
  group_by(population) %>%
  summarize(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_mao = sum(!is.na(mao)),
    mean_mao = mean(mao, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_offer = mean(offer, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ug_summary
```

Before: one row per participant. After: one row per population. Elite versus
undergraduate status was not randomly assigned; this is a descriptive comparison.
If you use `group_by(elite)` instead, the two groups are identical in `ug`.

## Grouping persists until removed

```{r}
year_incumbency <- elections %>%
  group_by(year, inc3) %>%
  summarize(n_races = n(), mean_dv = mean(dv))
group_vars(year_incumbency)
year_incumbency %>% slice_max(n_races, n = 1) %>% head()
year_incumbency %>% ungroup() %>% slice_max(n_races, n = 1)
```

With one summary row per group, the default drops the last grouping variable,
leaving `year`. Thus the first `slice_max()` finds a maximum **per year**.
Use `ungroup()` or `.groups = "drop"` when subsequent operations should be global.

## Grouped `mutate()` preserves participant rows

```{r}
ug_centered <- ug %>%
  group_by(population) %>%
  mutate(
    group_mean = mean(mao, na.rm = TRUE),
    mao_centered = mao - group_mean
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
ug_centered %>% select(participant_id, population, mao, group_mean, mao_centered) %>% head()
```

`summarize()` makes group-level rows. `mutate()` adds group-based calculations
to the original participant rows. Do not average group means without thinking
about group sizes and the target population.

## Revisit B2's empirical PMF

```{r}
mao_pmf <- ug %>%
  filter(!is.na(mao)) %>%
  count(population, mao, name = "frequency") %>%
  group_by(population) %>%
  mutate(probability = frequency / sum(frequency)) %>%
  ungroup()
mao_pmf %>% filter(mao %in% c(0, 25, 50))
mao_pmf %>% group_by(population) %>% summarize(total = sum(probability))
```

`count(population, mao)` is a shortcut for grouped row counts. The denominator
is the number of **observed MAOs within that population**, not all 234 people.
Missingness is excluded explicitly for this empirical distribution.

**Try it:** Add an empirical CDF using `arrange(mao)` and
`mutate(cdf = cumsum(probability))` *within each population*. Check that the
final CDF value is 1. This is the same probability calculation as B2.

# 4. Character strings

The book's string tools are handy for labels and inspection. They are not a
substitute for a validated identifier when merging people.

```{r}
ca_names <- members %>% filter(state_abbrev == "CA") %>% select(icpsr, bioname)
ca_names %>% filter(str_detect(bioname, "SÁNCHEZ|PELOSI"))
ca_names %>% mutate(surname = str_extract(bioname, "^[^,]+")) %>% head()
```

`|` means OR in this regular expression. `^` anchors the beginning;
`[^,]+` matches one or more characters other than a comma. This extracts the
text before the first comma; it is a display label, not a unique person ID.

The remaining tools in PSD §6.5, with real member names:

```{r}
name_examples <- ca_names$bioname[1:3]
length(name_examples)                 # Number of strings
str_length(name_examples)             # Characters in each string
str_count(name_examples, ",")         # Number of commas in each string
str_extract(name_examples, "[A-Z]")   # First ASCII capital letter
str_extract_all(name_examples, "[A-Z]") # All matches: a list
str_remove_all(name_examples, "[aeiou]") # A text operation, not name cleaning
str_split(name_examples, ",")         # List of vectors
str_split_fixed(name_examples, ",", n = 2) # Matrix with two columns
str_flatten(name_examples, collapse = "; ") # One display string
```

Do not treat `[A-Z]` as an inclusive definition of letters in names: accents,
non-Latin scripts, suffixes, and naming conventions all matter. Nor does this
extract-all example compute initials (the surnames here are uppercase).

Column-selection helpers can also match names:

```{r}
members %>% select(state_abbrev, bioname, matches("^nominate_")) %>% head()
```

# 5. Changing the shape of a table

## Wide and long representations

The UG table is useful with one row per person and separate `mao` and `offer`
columns. For a comparison across *choice types*, use one row per person-choice.
Neither shape is inherently wrong: define the unit needed for the question.

```{r}
ug_long <- ug %>%
  select(participant_id, population, mao, offer) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mao, offer),
    names_to = "choice", values_to = "amount"
  )
ug_long %>% head(n = 8)
```

The column names become values of `choice`. Their contents become `amount`.
There are now 468 rows, **still 234 people**. We retained missing amounts;
`values_drop_na = TRUE` would remove those rows, which is not the same as zero.

```{r}
choice_summary <- ug_long %>%
  group_by(population, choice) %>%
  summarize(n_observed = sum(!is.na(amount)),
            mean_amount = mean(amount, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
choice_summary
```

## Widen a summary for presentation

```{r}
choice_summary %>%
  select(population, choice, mean_amount) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = population, names_from = choice, values_from = mean_amount)
```

Each population-choice key must identify one value. Do not ask `pivot_wider()`
to silently average multiple people into one cell. Summarize first when that
is the intended calculation. `values_fill = 0` is appropriate only when an
absent combination means zero, not an unrecorded response or unknown mean.

Recover the person-level wide data without losing missingness:

```{r}
ug_wide_again <- ug_long %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(participant_id, population),
              names_from = choice, values_from = amount)
stopifnot(nrow(ug_wide_again) == nrow(ug))
```

# 6. Append observations with `bind_rows()`

`turk` has one row per MTurk respondent, with the repeated elite block already
excluded. Align the common variables, then stack the observations:

```{r}
all_ug <- bind_rows(
  ug %>% select(participant_id, population, elite, mao, offer, age),
  turk %>% select(participant_id, population, elite, mao, offer, age)
)
all_ug %>% count(population)
all_ug %>% filter(!is.na(mao)) %>% count(population)
```

The second count reproduces B2: 98 elites, 130 undergraduates, 1,006 MTurk
respondents. Retaining missing MAOs yields 1,241 rows instead of B2's 1,234.

`bind_rows()` adds observations and aligns columns by name. A join matches
keys and attaches information. The original UG files have no validated shared
participant ID for a general person-level join. Equal MAOs or equal row numbers
across separate files are not evidence of a match.

After appending, `elite == 0` pools **two different comparison samples**.
Use `population` when you want to keep undergraduates and MTurk separate.

# 7. Join elections to Voteview

## First a simple lookup

The source codebook defines `state` as alphabetical position among the 50
states. `states.csv` is the matching lookup from R's state names/abbreviations.
It is not a crosswalk between numeric FIPS and ICPSR codes.

```{r}
states %>% head()
elections_2014 <- elections %>%
  filter(year == 2014) %>%
  mutate(district = stcd %% 100, congress = 114) %>%
  left_join(states, by = "state", relationship = "many-to-one")
elections_2014 %>% select(year, state_name, district, dv) %>% head()
```

`%% 100` takes the remainder after division by 100: `1304` becomes district 4.
The 2014 election precedes the **114th Congress, 2015–2017**. We are describing
the district's subsequent representation, not its incumbent before the election.

## Check the keys before the substantive join

Voteview has one record per member appearance in a Congress. Some districts
had replacements during the term. `state_abbrev + district_code` is therefore
not necessarily unique, even after filtering to House members in Congress 114.

```{r}
duplicate_districts <- members %>%
  count(state_abbrev, district_code) %>%
  filter(n > 1)
duplicate_districts

members %>%
  filter(state_abbrev == "IL", district_code == 18) %>%
  select(bioname, nominate_dim1)
```

A raw left join illustrates the consequence:

```{r}
raw_join <- elections_2014 %>%
  left_join(members, by = c("congress", "state_abbrev", "district" = "district_code"))
c(before = nrow(elections_2014), after = nrow(raw_join))
```

328 election rows become 333 matched rows. A left join retains every left
observation, but **does not promise the same number of rows**. No warning is
required for a one-to-many join. Repeating the election outcome gives those
districts extra weight in later calculations.

## A conservative classroom rule

Keep a NOMINATE match only if exactly one member record is available for the
district in that Congress. Leave ambiguous election rows unmatched; do not
claim the person with the first row or largest score was the election winner.

```{r}
members_unique <- members %>%
  group_by(congress, state_abbrev, district_code) %>%
  filter(n() == 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(congress, state_abbrev, district_code, icpsr, bioname, nominate_dim1)

joined <- elections_2014 %>%
  left_join(members_unique,
            by = c("congress", "state_abbrev", "district" = "district_code"),
            relationship = "many-to-one")

joined %>% select(year, state_abbrev, district, dv, bioname, nominate_dim1) %>% head()
stopifnot(nrow(joined) == nrow(elections_2014))
```

`relationship = "many-to-one"` checks that each left row matches at most one
right row. It requires dplyr 1.1.0 or later. It does **not** check whether a
match exists, whether the key is substantively correct, or whether a matched
score is missing.

## Audit unmatched keys and missing measurements separately

```{r}
unmatched <- anti_join(elections_2014, members_unique,
                      by = c("congress", "state_abbrev", "district" = "district_code"))
unmatched %>% select(state_abbrev, district, dv)

joined %>% summarize(
  rows = n(),
  no_member_match = sum(is.na(icpsr)),
  matched_but_missing_score = sum(!is.na(icpsr) & is.na(nominate_dim1))
)
```

The five unmatched election rows are the ambiguous districts HI-1, IL-18,
KY-1, MS-1, and PA-2. The sixth duplicate district in Voteview, OH-8, is absent
from the selected elections CSV. No election row was discarded by the safe join.

For another year, recheck the Congress, district boundaries, at-large coding,
and duplicate records. Do not extrapolate this one-year merge automatically.

## Other join choices

```{r}
inner_result <- inner_join(elections_2014, members_unique,
                          by = c("congress", "state_abbrev", "district" = "district_code"))
semi_result <- semi_join(elections_2014, members_unique,
                        by = c("congress", "state_abbrev", "district" = "district_code"))
c(left = nrow(joined), inner = nrow(inner_result), semi = nrow(semi_result))
```

| Join | What remains? |
|---|---|
| `left_join(x, y)` | Every left row, with right-side fields where keys match |
| `inner_join(x, y)` | Matched keys only; adds right-side fields |
| `right_join(x, y)` | Every right row, plus matching left-side information |
| `full_join(x, y)` | Keys from either side, with missing fields as needed |
| `semi_join(x, y)` | Left rows with a match, without adding right-side fields |
| `anti_join(x, y)` | Left rows without a match |

## Describe the merged data

```{r}
plot_data <- joined %>% filter(!is.na(nominate_dim1))
plot(plot_data$dv, plot_data$nominate_dim1,
     xlab = "Democratic two-party vote, 2014 (%)",
     ylab = "Representative's first-dimension NOMINATE score",
     pch = 19, col = "#005a8b88")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70", lty = 2)
```

This describes retained district elections and unambiguous subsequent member
records. The first dimension broadly orders liberal–conservative roll-call
positions; it is not an ideological scale for the district's voters. The plot
does not identify a causal effect of votes on ideology. NOMINATE values are
estimates in the current frozen release, not forecasts available in 2014.

# 8. Save a result

Use a new filename rather than overwriting raw input:

```{r}
#| eval: false
write_csv(joined, "elections-2014-with-nominate.csv")
```

Keep the script or QMD that produced it. An exported table alone does not
record the exclusions, definitions, and join rules that created it.

# 9. Optional reference: the apply family

PSD §6.7 provides an alternative way to repeat calculations. You already used
`replicate()` for repeated simulations. Here `apply()` works on rows or columns;
`sapply()` applies a function to elements of a vector/list and tries to simplify.

```{r}
amounts <- as.matrix(select(ug, mao, offer))
apply(amounts, MARGIN = 2, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
# This repeats mean() for each column. MARGIN = 1 would operate per row.

offer_values <- c(20, 30, 40, 50)
acceptance <- sapply(offer_values, function(o) mean(ug$mao <= o, na.rm = TRUE))
tibble(offer = offer_values, acceptance,
       expected_payoff = (100 - offer_values) * acceptance)
```

The acceptance calculation pools the observed MAOs in these two samples,
with weight proportional to sample size. It is not a population-weighted estimate
for society. In a real analysis, choose and defend the population first.

Avoid `apply()` on a mixed numeric/character data frame: coercing it to a
matrix can turn all columns into strings. `sapply()` can return different
shapes depending on the results. `lapply()` always returns a list; `vapply()`
lets you specify the expected output type. Those distinctions are reference
material, not a second programming curriculum for today.

  [grouping](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/grouping.html),
  and [join documentation](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate-joins.html).
- [tidyr pivoting](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/pivot.html) and
  [stringr introduction](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/articles/stringr.html).
- Jacobson, Gary (2015), *It's Nothing Personal: The Decline of the Incumbency
  Advantage in U.S. House Elections*, [replication archive](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/29559).
  The course CSV is a selected extract, checked against the aggregate archive.
- LeVeck et al. (2014), *The Role of Self Interest in Elite Bargaining*,
  [replication archive](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/27894). See `data/SOURCES.txt`.
- Lewis et al. (2026), [Voteview](https://voteview.com/),
  [member-file documentation](https://voteview.com/articles/data_help_members).
  Frozen download: October 20, 2026; teaching subset: House, Congress 114.

For an individual function, type `?filter`, `?pivot_longer`, or `?left_join`
in the Console. If a different package masks a function, use its explicit name,
such as `dplyr::filter()`.
